Q: Google OAuth: "Couldn't sign you in. This browser or app may not be secure." A:

1. The script imports necessary modules from PySide6 for creating a web application.

2. It defines a URL for Google's OAuth Playground to simulate a "Sign in with Google" process without using secrets.

3. The main function initializes a QApplication and sets up a QWebEngineProfile to modify the user agent string.

4. A QWebEngineView is created to display the Google sign-in page, with specified dimensions, and the application runs until closed.

5. The script is intended to demonstrate a Google sign-in process using PySide6 and QtWebEngine, but actual login will be blocked.

Q: Issue using JSON_MODIFY with JSON_QUERY in a CASE expression A:

The problem with your approach (using JSON_MODIFY) is escaping. As is explained in the documentation ...JSON_MODIFY escapes all special characters in the new value if the type of the value is varchar or nvarchar. A text value isn't escaped if it's properly formatted JSON produced by FOR JSON, JSON_QUERY, or JSON_MODIFY ... . In your situation, if you want to generate a valid JSON content, you need to consider the escaping. Using REPLACE() to build the expected JSON output from text content may result in invalid or wrong JSON.

A possible solution here is to make one additional check for stored ordinary string. You simply need to transform it as JSON array ("plain-string" into ["plain-string"]) and check it again with ISJSON(). In case of invalid JSON, the JSON_MODIFY() function will escape it.

Note, that starting from SQL Server 2025, you may use JSON_OBJECT() to build a JSON object.

SELECT *
INTO #JsonTable
FROM (VALUES
    (0, '{"sample":"object"}'),
    (1, '"plain-string-escaped-JSON"'),
    (2, ':plain-string"-unescaped-JSON\')
) v (Id, JsonValue)


SELECT 
    JsonValue2016 = CASE
        WHEN ISJSON(JsonValue) = 1 THEN JSON_MODIFY('{}',  '$.Values', JSON_QUERY(JsonValue))
        WHEN ISJSON('[' + JsonValue + ']') = 1 THEN JSON_MODIFY('{}',  '$.Values', JSON_VALUE('[' + JsonValue + ']', '$[0]'))
        ELSE JSON_MODIFY('{}',  '$.Values', JsonValue)
    END,
    JsonValue2025 = CASE
        WHEN ISJSON(JsonValue) = 1 THEN JSON_OBJECT('Values': JSON_QUERY(JsonValue))
        WHEN ISJSON('[' + JsonValue + ']') = 1 THEN JSON_OBJECT('Values': JSON_VALUE('[' + JsonValue + ']', '$[0]'))
        ELSE JSON_OBJECT('Values': JsonValue)
    END
FROM #JsonTable

Result

JsonValue2016 JsonValue2025
{"Values":{"sample":"object"}} {"Values":{"sample":"object"}}
{"Values":"plain-string-escaped-JSON"} {"Values":"plain-string-escaped-JSON"}
{"Values":":plain-string\"-unescaped-JSON\\"} {"Values":":plain-string\"-unescaped-JSON\\"}

Q: Why am I forced to use gawk paragraph mode here? A:

learned then about "paragraph mode"

From Multiple-Line Records in The GNU Awk User’s Guide

Another technique is to have blank lines separate records. By a special dispensation, an empty string as the value of RS indicates that records are separated by one or more blank lines. When RS is set to the empty string, each record always ends at the first blank line encountered. The next record doesn’t start until the first nonblank line that follows. No matter how many blank lines appear in a row, they all act as one record separator. (Blank lines must be completely empty; lines that contain only whitespace do not count.)

You can achieve the same effect as RS = "" by assigning the string " +" to RS. This regexp matches the newline at the end of the record and one or more blank lines after the record. In addition, a regular expression always matches the longest possible sequence when there is a choice(...)the next record doesn’t start until the first nonblank line that follows—no matter how many blank lines appear in a row, they are considered one record separator.

However, there is an important difference between RS = "" and RS = " +". In the first case, leading newlines in the input data file are ignored, and if a file ends without extra blank lines after the last record, the final newline is removed from the record. In the second case, this special processing is not done.

Described difference can be shown following way

printf '

A

B

C
' | awk 'BEGIN{RS=""}END{print NR}'

does output 3, whilst

printf '

A

B

C
' | awk 'BEGIN{RS="

+"}END{print NR}'

does output 4.

(tested in GNU Awk 5.3.1)

Q: What does information_schema.TABLES.DATA_FREE mean in MySQL? A:

DATA_FREE- The number of allocated but unused bytes. It is the size of the database files compared to the data stored in the database files. PHPMyAdmin shows this information as 'Overhead in tables'.

However for InnoDB this is important- "InnoDB tables report the free space of the tablespace to which the table belongs. For a table located in the shared tablespace, this is the free space of the shared tablespace.". So with a typical InnoDB setup (innodb_file_per_table is not set) you will get the free space for all tables and not for a single table.

Refer: http://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/5.5/en/tables-table.html and http://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/5.5/en/show-table-status.html
